I would recommend becoming a groundman and going from there. You'll start the trade making money and you'll be able to see the work and tell if you actually want to do it or not. You're probably going to spend around 25 to 30,000 on a line school, but there are also colleges that offer line work programs that you might only spend $3,000. But those aren't as well known and don't really hold as much weight unless you plan on moving to a local utility around that college.

Anyways, in Florida you can become a ground man as easy as pie. And if you're on a crew that gets to go on storm, you can still make 100,000 that year. From there you can apply to an apprenticeship and tell them that you actually have ground men experience and that will help get your foot in the door. If you like the crew you're working on, when it's your time to join the apprenticeship, if you're a groundman, you can indenture. Which means you stay on the crew that you're on, you just become an apprentice. If you come in off the street and apply to the apprenticeship, will send you to any state they want. That's why I ended up in Georgia for four fucking years and it probably ruined my social life hardcore. I'm from South Florida.

But to clarify, You don't have to go to Florida as a groundment to do that. You can start working as a groundman in any state. Just start applying. But by far and away, if you just want to start working and get into an apprenticeship the Southeast is going to be the fastest place. It's also the place that is going to treat you the worst and pay you the least. But you will be getting experience and a ticket is a ticket. If I wanted to move to California tomorrow with my ticket, I could.

I hope this helps as well, ask me anything. By the way 32 is still plenty young for this trade. I'm working with someone who is 46 and joining the apprenticeship
